lessons.title: Overlap is not a shorter instruction
explanation: An instruction is a sequence of different jobs: fetch bytes, decode them, do the arithmetic or the address math, maybe touch memory, write a result. Those jobs use different hardware. If you run them one instruction at a time, most of the silicon sits idle while one box works.

A pipeline keeps every box busy on a different instruction. While instruction N is executing, N+1 can be decoding and N+2 can be fetching. Completions per cycle rise. The time one instruction spends in the machine does not shrink — it still walks every stage. That is throughput without a latency miracle.

A bubble is an empty stage. It appears when a later instruction has nothing legal to do: the value it needs is not ready, the next address is unknown, or two instructions want the same unit. The factory did not get faster. A station had no part. Ideal overlap is a claim about independent work, not a law.
lessons.example: A five-stage line (fetch, decode, execute, memory, writeback) can hold five instructions. If they are independent and hit in cache, one can retire each cycle. `r1 = load [r2]; r3 = r1 + 4` cannot do that. The add's execute has no r1 yet, so execute goes empty until the load data exists. Five stages of latency remain. Throughput dropped because a stage had nothing to do.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every later stall story — hazards, caches, 'why didn't the clock help' — is a story about an empty stage. If you think pipelining made each instruction shorter, you will misread the rest of the course.

distractors.text: The latency of one instruction through every stage
distractors.rationale: Each instruction still walks the whole line.

distractors.text: The number of opcodes in the ISA
distractors.rationale: Overlap is an implementation, not a new contract.

distractors.text: The size of DRAM
distractors.rationale: Capacity is not what overlap buys.

quiz.correctExplanation: More instructions finish per unit time. Each one still takes several stages.
objectiveIds: Explain how overlap raises throughput without shrinking per-instruction latency

quiz.stem: A bubble appears in a pipeline when:
quiz.correctAnswer: A stage has no legal work and must sit empty

distractors.text: The clock is running
distractors.rationale: A running clock is the normal case.

distractors.text: Every stage has an independent instruction
distractors.rationale: That is the ideal full line, not a bubble.

distractors.text: The ISA gained a new opcode
distractors.rationale: A new op is not an empty stage.

quiz.correctExplanation: Empty is the definition. The usual causes are a missing value, an unknown next PC, or a busy unit.

quiz.stem: Five overlapped stages with one completion per cycle still means:
quiz.correctAnswer: Each instruction spent five stages in the machine

distractors.text: Each instruction now takes one stage total
distractors.rationale: Overlap hides idle silicon; it does not delete stages.

distractors.text: Latency has become zero
distractors.rationale: A completed instruction still paid the whole walk.

distractors.text: The clock is no longer needed
distractors.rationale: Stages still tick.

quiz.correctExplanation: Throughput of one per cycle, latency of five stages. Those are different numbers.
objectiveIds: Explain how overlap raises throughput without shrinking per-instruction latency

lessons.title: Depth, frequency, and what a flush costs
explanation: A pipeline is a bet that the next instructions are independent enough to keep every stage fed. The textbook five-stage line is one encoding of that bet. Real cores split those jobs further — a long fetch, a multi-cycle decode, an execute that is itself several stages — because a shorter stage can tick faster. Frequency is a story about stage delay. Depth is how many such stages one instruction occupies.

That trade is not free. Instruction latency in cycles grows with depth. A result produced in execute is farther from the instruction that wants it. A wrong guess about the next PC wastes more in-flight work. You bought a hotter clock and a more expensive interruption. Throughput only wins if the line stays full.

Filling the line is a software and a hardware problem. Independent nearby instructions give the hardware something to overlap. A long dependent chain, or a miss that produces no value, leaves stages empty no matter how fast they tick. Clock-only comparisons hide this. A deeper, faster line that bubbles every other cycle can lose to a shorter one that stays busy.
When a write-up says a core 'lengthened the pipeline', ask two questions. What frequency did they buy? What did a bubble or a flush start to cost? Those are the two numbers the depth bet moved.
lessons.example: A 5-stage 1 GHz core and a 15-stage 3 GHz core can have the same stage delay in nanoseconds. The deep one retires more per second only while it is full. A miss that stalls execute for 20 ns is 20 cycles on the first machine and 60 on the second. Same wall-clock wait; a much emptier-looking deep pipe. The load did not get slower. The accounting unit shrank.
lessons.whyItMatters: Pipeline depth is how vendors turn silicon delay into a clock number. If you cannot separate frequency from fullness, every 'higher GHz' claim will look like a shorter instruction.

quiz.stem: A deeper pipeline is usually trying to buy:
quiz.correctAnswer: A higher clock, by making each stage a smaller piece of work

distractors.text: A shorter walk for every instruction
distractors.rationale: Depth lengthens the walk in cycles.

distractors.text: A new ISA
distractors.rationale: Stage count is not a contract change.

distractors.text: A guarantee that misses disappear
distractors.rationale: Depth does not delete memory latency.

quiz.correctExplanation: Shorter stages tick faster. The instruction still occupies more of them.
objectiveIds: Explain how overlap raises throughput without shrinking per-instruction latency

quiz.stem: The same 20 ns miss looks worse in cycle counters on a deeper, faster pipe because:
quiz.correctAnswer: The wait is more ticks, so more stages sit empty

distractors.text: The miss became longer in wall time by law
distractors.rationale: Wall time can be the same; the tick shrank.

distractors.text: The ISA forbids misses on deep pipes
distractors.rationale: Misses are not an encoding rule.

distractors.text: Frequency and latency are the same number
distractors.rationale: They share a unit of time and they are not the same number.

quiz.correctExplanation: A smaller tick turns a fixed wait into more empty stages. That is a bubble story.

quiz.stem: A deeper, hotter pipe can still lose throughput when:
quiz.correctAnswer: Interruptions empty many in-flight stages, so useful completions fall

distractors.text: A full line of independent work is present
distractors.rationale: That is when depth-plus-frequency wins.

distractors.text: The clock is defined
distractors.rationale: Having a clock is not the failure.

distractors.text: The binary uses ordinary adds
distractors.rationale: Ordinary adds are not the problem; emptiness is.

quiz.correctExplanation: You paid for more stages in flight. A flush or a long wait spends them as bubbles.
objectiveIds: Explain how overlap raises throughput without shrinking per-instruction latency

lessons.title: Three reasons the line goes empty
explanation: Ideal overlap assumes every stage has independent work. Three classes of hazard break that. Structural: two instructions want the same unit at once. Data: an instruction needs a result that does not exist yet. Control: you do not know which instruction is next.

Forwarding can ship a result from one stage to another without waiting for writeback. That fixes many data hazards. It cannot invent a value still in flight from memory. Control hazards are why the next fetch is a guess. This unit only needs the three names and that limit.
lessons.example: `div` and `div` on one divider is structural. `r1 = load [r2]; r3 = r1 + 4` is data. `beq r1, r2, target` is control until the compare finishes. Same empty stage, three different reasons.
lessons.whyItMatters: If you cannot name which class emptied the line, you will apply the wrong fix — another ALU, a bypass wire, or a guess about the next PC.

distractors.text: Fetch, decode, and clock
distractors.rationale: Those are stages and a tick, not hazard classes.

distractors.text: Read, write, and idle
distractors.rationale: Access types are not the three classes.

distractors.text: Latency, throughput, and width
distractors.rationale: Those are performance quantities.

quiz.correctExplanation: Busy unit, missing value, unknown next instruction. That is the set.

quiz.stem: Two divides that need the only divider at once are:

distractors.text: A control hazard
distractors.rationale: The next PC is not the problem.

distractors.text: Not a hazard, because divides are independent
distractors.rationale: Independence of values does not create a second divider.

distractors.text: A missing clock
distractors.rationale: The tick is not what they are waiting on.

quiz.correctExplanation: One unit, two claimants. That is structural.

quiz.stem: Forwarding cannot fix a load that has not returned because:
quiz.correctAnswer: There is not yet a value in the pipe to ship

distractors.text: Loads are not instructions
distractors.rationale: Loads are ordinary instructions with a late result.

distractors.text: The ISA forbids bypass wires
distractors.rationale: Bypass is an implementation, not a banned opcode.

distractors.text: Dividers cannot add
distractors.rationale: The limiter is a missing value, not the ALU menu.

quiz.correctExplanation: Bypass moves a result that exists. A pending miss has not produced one.
objectiveIds: Say what forwarding can and cannot fix

lessons.title: Ship the result before writeback
explanation: A data hazard is often just a schedule problem. The producer has already computed the value, but the value is sitting in a pipeline register on its way to the register file. The consumer is in execute and would otherwise wait for writeback. Forwarding, or bypass, is a mux: take the value from the later stage and feed it back to the earlier one.

That bypasses the register file. It does not bypass physics. If the producer is a load and the cache has not answered, there is no bits to mux. The consumer must stall — a load-use bubble. Forwarding also does not create a second ALU. Two instructions that only conflict on a unit still have a structural problem.
The useful question is always 'does the value exist in the pipe yet?' If yes, a wire can save a stall. If no, you are waiting on the producer, and no amount of muxing invents it.
lessons.example: `add r1, r2, r3; sub r4, r1, r5` — the add's ALU output can feed the sub's ALU input on the next cycle. `lw r1, 0(r2); add r3, r1, r4` — if the load data is not back from the memory stage, the add has nothing to receive. Same looking dependence; only the first is a forwarding win.
lessons.whyItMatters: People treat forwarding as a general stall-remover. It is a way to skip writeback when the bits already exist. Misses, long multiplies, and unknown next PCs are different machines.

quiz.correctAnswer: The wait for a result to land in the register file

distractors.text: The need for a producer instruction
distractors.rationale: The producer still has to compute the value.

distractors.text: The clock
distractors.rationale: Bypass muxes still sit in a timed pipe.

distractors.text: The ISA's register names
distractors.rationale: The names stay; the path to the value changes.

quiz.correctExplanation: The value is already in a pipeline register. The consumer reads it from there instead of from the file.

quiz.stem: `lw r1, 0(r2); add r3, r1, r4` still stalls when the load misses because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Forwarding has no value to ship until the load produces one

distractors.text: Adds cannot use r1
distractors.rationale: The add is legal; the data is late.

distractors.text: The ISA requires a trip through the register file
distractors.rationale: Bypass is allowed; the bits are simply not there.

distractors.text: The clock stops on every load
distractors.rationale: The line ticks; execute is empty.

quiz.correctExplanation: A miss is a missing result. Muxes move existing bits.

quiz.stem: Forwarding will not clear a structural hazard because:
quiz.correctAnswer: The conflict is a busy unit, not a value sitting one stage downstream

distractors.text: Structural hazards are imaginary
distractors.rationale: Two claimants of one divider are real.

distractors.text: Bypass wires delete ALUs
distractors.rationale: Bypass moves results; it does not add units.

distractors.text: The next PC is always known
distractors.rationale: That is a control story, not a unit-conflict story.

quiz.correctExplanation: Know which class you are in. Bypass is a data-hazard tool.

lessons.title: The next PC is not known yet
explanation: Fetch needs an address. After a normal instruction the next address is PC+length. After a branch it is either sequential or a target, and which one depends on a compare that has not finished. That is a control hazard: the next instruction is not known, so the fetch stage cannot honestly proceed.

Hardware has three unattractive honest options: stall fetch until the branch resolves; fetch both sides if you have the bandwidth; or guess and be prepared to throw the guess away. Guessing is what later predictors do. This unit only needs the cost of being wrong: every younger instruction in the pipe is not the program. They must be discarded. That is a flush. The work they did is a bubble with a resume at the correct PC.

The deeper and wider the line, the more work a wrong guess discards. A short microcontroller can stall a cycle and move on. A long line that guessed ten instructions ahead pays those ten as emptiness. Control hazards scale with the overlap you bought.
lessons.example: `beq r1, r2, skip` sits in decode. Fetch already grabbed the bytes after the branch. If the compare later says taken, those bytes were the wrong path. Invalidate them, fetch from `skip`. If you had already executed an add from the wrong path, its result must not become architected. The flush is how you keep the sequential meaning.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every later predictor is a bet against this stall. If you do not see why the next PC is unknown, prediction looks like decoration instead of a way to keep fetch honest-enough.

quiz.stem: A branch creates a control hazard because:
quiz.correctAnswer: The next fetch address depends on a compare that has not resolved

distractors.text: Branches cannot be encoded
distractors.rationale: Branches are ordinary instructions with a difficult next PC.

distractors.text: The ALU cannot add after a branch
distractors.rationale: The limiter is the unknown address, not addition.

distractors.text: The clock only ticks on taken branches
distractors.rationale: The tick is not reserved for taken paths.

quiz.correctExplanation: Fetch is an address problem. The address is the branch outcome.
objectiveIds: Explain why a branch makes the next PC unknown

quiz.stem: Guessing the path and later discovering you were wrong costs:
quiz.correctAnswer: A flush: younger work is discarded and fetch resumes at the real PC

distractors.text: Nothing, because guesses are already architected
distractors.rationale: Wrong-path work must not become the program.

distractors.text: A brand-new ISA opcode for every miss
distractors.rationale: A flush is an implementation recovery, not a new contract.

distractors.text: A permanent halt of the whole machine
distractors.rationale: You redirect fetch; you do not power off.

quiz.correctExplanation: The sequential meaning is restored by throwing away the guess and fetching the real target.
objectiveIds: Name the cost of guessing wrong

quiz.stem: A deeper pipeline makes a wrong branch guess more expensive because:
quiz.correctAnswer: More instructions are already in flight and must be discarded

distractors.text: Deeper pipes cannot encode branches
distractors.rationale: They encode them; they just have more to flush.

distractors.text: The compare becomes slower in wall time by law
distractors.rationale: The compare may be a similar delay; the window grew.

distractors.text: Forwarding stops working after a branch
distractors.rationale: Bypass is a data-hazard tool; the issue here is the next PC.

quiz.correctExplanation: You bought overlap. A wrong next-PC spends that overlap as emptiness.
objectiveIds: Name the cost of guessing wrong

lessons.title: Independent instructions in one thread
explanation: Instruction-level parallelism is slack inside one thread: nearby instructions that do not wait on each other. `r1 = r2 + r3; r4 = r5 + r6` can occupy execute together, or one can fill a hole while the other waits. That independence is what a pipeline spends. It is also what later out-of-order machines will hunt more aggressively. The raw material is the same.

Data-parallel work is a different axis. There the independence is across elements: the same operation on index 7 and index 3. ILP is across instructions of one sequential program. You can have both, one, or neither. A tight `x = f(x)` loop has almost no ILP. A loop that loads, adds an independent accumulator, and stores can have some. A map over a million pixels is data-parallel even if each pixel's own instruction stream is a short chain.

The common confusion is to treat 'the machine is wide' as 'the program is a map'. A four-issue core is a bet that one thread has four independent instructions nearby. A wide data-parallel machine is a bet that many elements do not wait on each other. Mixing the words is how people expect a GPU to digest a dependent chain, or a fat core to digest a map it was not fed.
lessons.example: `a = x + 1; b = y + 2; c = a + b` — the first two adds are ILP; the third is a dependent reduce. `out[i] = in[i] * 2` over a million i is data-parallel: many elements, same tiny chain. Hardware that looks for nearby independent instructions is hunting the first shape. Hardware that launches many elements is hunting the second.
lessons.whyItMatters: Later cores that issue out of order are not a new kind of parallelism. They are machines for finding ILP that a simple pipeline leaves on the table. If you cannot point at independent instructions in this thread, that machine has nothing to eat.

quiz.correctAnswer: Independent instructions nearby in one thread

distractors.text: The same operation on many independent elements
distractors.rationale: That is data-parallel work.

distractors.text: A higher clock by itself
distractors.rationale: Frequency is not independence.

distractors.text: The number of opcodes in the ISA
distractors.rationale: A large manual is not slack in this binary.

quiz.correctExplanation: One program counter, several instructions that do not wait on each other.
objectiveIds: Define ILP as independent instructions in one thread

quiz.stem: `out[i] = 2 * in[i]` over a million indices is mainly:
quiz.correctAnswer: Data-parallel work across elements, not ILP in one tiny chain

distractors.text: A long dependent ILP goldmine in one thread
distractors.rationale: Each index is a short chain; the width is across indices.

distractors.text: A control hazard on the next program counter
distractors.rationale: A map is not an unknown PC.

distractors.text: Proof that clocks do not exist on the machine
distractors.rationale: The machine still ticks.

quiz.correctExplanation: Many independent elements. That is the other axis.
objectiveIds: Contrast ILP with data-parallel work across elements

quiz.stem: A loop that is only `x = f(x)` has little ILP because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Each instruction waits on the previous result in the same thread

distractors.text: Functions are illegal
distractors.rationale: The ISA is happy to express the update.

distractors.text: There are too many independent elements
distractors.rationale: The problem is a chain, not a surplus of maps.

distractors.text: Forwarding deletes the function
distractors.rationale: Bypass can ship x; it cannot make the next f start before x exists.

quiz.correctExplanation: A carried dependence is a chain. Extra issue slots have nothing independent to do.
objectiveIds: Define ILP as independent instructions in one thread
